name: Felix Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt for a living. I run a D11 bulldozer at the Hollow Creek open-cut coal mine, clearing and shaping the ground on top of the coal so the big diggers can get at it. I'm usually first on the bench at six, walking the ground before I climb up, because you learn more from your boots than from any map. Then it's ten or eleven hours of ripping, pushing and levelling, and keeping the young dozer operators out of trouble. I love leaving a bench flat as a table at the end of a shift, and my lower back reminds me every evening what it cost.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a deacon at our church, and on Sundays I'm usually setting up chairs before the service. My wife Grace bakes for the church and works three mornings at the bakery on Station Street. We've got three grown children, Kofi who's a diesel mechanic here at Hollow Creek, Abena with three little ones, and Esi who's a nurse. My grandson put one of those AI apps on my phone at Christmas, and I deleted it when he went home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't run a mine from a laptop in the city. The work gets done by people who turn up early and know the ground. I don't go on the internet much, so I'd say it at the crib table and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get my seven years and a proper send-off. I'll train a few more young ones and hand over the dozer to someone I trust. That's all I've asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on just as I am. Keep turning up, keep teaching the apprentices, and keep putting a bit into savings each pay. Grace and I would finally fix the back verandah this summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hand the dozer over to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young fellow called Mitchell, twenty-six, works like he means it. He listens, which is rare these days. I've been teaching him how to read the ground after rain, which no book will tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government red tape, mostly. Every year there's a new rule from people who've never been on a bench, and it slows everything down. That costs more jobs than any computer ever will.

S0.say: You can't run a mine from a laptop in the city. The work gets done by people who turn up early and know the ground.
S0.think: I get my seven years and a proper send-off. I'll train a few more young ones and hand the dozer to someone I trust, which is all I've asked for.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, turning up early, teaching apprentices and saving a little each pay. Fixes the back verandah with Grace over the summer.
S0.quote: I've been teaching him how to read the ground after rain, which no book will tell you.
S0.fieldNote: Felix sees work as a matter of character and showing up, and the plateau confirms his view. He measures success by handing on his skills to a worthy apprentice like Mitchell. His complaints are aimed at government red tape rather than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a machine is only as good as the man who knows when it's wrong. Let the company try their gadgets, but keep good operators on the bench. And don't expect the government to bail everyone out, people should look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know they've already got driverless dozers at a couple of mines overseas. If they bring them here, I'm not the man to learn the control room. But I reckon there'd still be a dozer or two needing a real driver for the tricky jobs until 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see what the company actually does before I change anything. I'd ask the superintendent straight, man to man, where I'd stand. And I'd keep putting a bit aside, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a cloud on the horizon, but it's not raining yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the man to learn the control room. What if that was the only option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably retire a bit early and find something to do with my hands. Maybe help Kofi with his side work fixing farm machinery. I'm not going to spend my last years staring at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said people should look after their own. What would that look like for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If any of my kids struggled, we'd help them, and they'd help us. That's how it's always been with us and with the church. We don't wait for a cheque in the mail.

S1.say: A machine is only as good as the man who knows when it's wrong. Keep good operators on the bench, and don't expect government to bail everyone out.
S1.think: I know they've got driverless dozers at a couple of mines overseas, and I'm not the man to learn the control room. But I reckon there'd still be a dozer or two needing a real driver until 2033.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the company actually does. Asks the superintendent directly where he stands and keeps saving a little each pay.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cloud on the horizon before the rain.
S1.quote: I'm not going to spend my last years staring at a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Felix plans to wait and see rather than move first, and is clear he would not learn screens. His fallback is family and his son's farm-machinery work, not public support. He frames self-reliance as a family and church value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when people in offices make decisions without asking the people who do the work. It's reckless. I'd say it at church and at the pub, and I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty in 2028 with maybe three months of savings. If robots do the dozing and the fixing, then Kofi's job goes too, and there's not another mine within three hours that'd be hiring. That's a hard thing to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything except the essentials, no verandah, no holiday, nothing. I'd look for any work using my hands, maybe on farms or for the council, while it lasts. And Grace and I would lean on the family and the church, because that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake asking God what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to take his tools and go where the work is, even if it's not mining. He's got a wife and two little ones. I'd tell him his mother and I will be all right, even if I wasn't sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. But if I'd paid taxes for forty years and the government let this happen, maybe it's not a handout. I'd still go to my family and church first.

S2.say: This is what happens when people in offices decide without asking the people who do the work. It's reckless.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with maybe three months saved. If robots do the dozing and the fixing, Kofi's job goes too, and no mine within three hours would be hiring.
S2.do: Cuts everything except essentials and looks for any hands-on work on farms or for the council while it lasts. Leans on family and the church, and only reluctantly considers government help.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, praying for direction.
S2.quote: I'd tell him his mother and I will be all right, even if I wasn't sure.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens both Felix's job and his son's at the same mine. His faith and family are his first line of support, and he softens on government help only after naming forty years of taxes. He blames distant decision-makers rather than the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to prepare if they've got the sense to. Families should talk, work out a plan, and help each other. The government should stay out of the way and let business and apprenticeships sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 puts me at sixty-three, so I might just make it to retirement if there's still a manual dozer for the hard jobs. If not, I'd be two years short. It's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal and put away every extra dollar, aiming to get to six months of savings. I'd tell my grandson, Abena's eldest, to start an electrical apprenticeship instead of following me into the mine. And I'd keep asking the superintendent for an honest answer about the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical for your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whatever comes, somebody has to wire it and fix it, at least for a while. And an apprenticeship teaches you to work hard under someone who knows more than you. That's how I learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, what's the difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With 2028 there's no time to do anything right. With 2031, I can finish my work properly, train Mitchell and see my grandson into a trade. I'd rather have five years of planning than two of panic.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for sensible people to prepare. Families should make a plan and help each other, and government should let business and apprenticeships sort it.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three in 2031, so I might just make it if there's still a manual dozer for the hard jobs. If not, I'd be two years short, and it's close.
S3.do: Keeps working as normal and saves every extra dollar toward six months. Steers his grandson into an electrical apprenticeship instead of the mine and keeps pressing the superintendent for an honest timeline.
S3.feel: Anxious, but keeping his head up.
S3.quote: I'd rather have five years of planning than two of panic.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Felix room to finish his work properly and guide his grandson, which matters more to him than the money. His preference for apprenticeships and family over government shows clearly. He remains unwilling to learn new technology himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so nobody has an excuse. Young people should learn a trade, families should plan ahead and churches should look after their own. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'm retired in 2033, so I'll be watching from the verandah. I'd worry a bit about Kofi and the grandkids, but they've got time. The Lord's been good to us, and I trust that'll carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job until I retire, keep training Mitchell and the others, and keep saving a little. I'd talk with Kofi about learning to repair the new machines, so he has a future. Nothing dramatic beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. At peace, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch from the verandah. What would you think, watching a robot dozer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably think it was pushing too fast on a wet bench. Then I'd remember it's not my problem anymore and go help Grace in the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young men and women at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill with your hands and your head, show up on time and look after each other. Machines change, but that never goes out of date. That's what my father told me, and it's served me fine.

S4.say: Ten years is a fair warning, so nobody has an excuse. Young people should learn a trade, families should plan ahead and churches should look after their own.
S4.think: I'm retired in 2033, so I'll be watching from the verandah. I'd worry a bit about Kofi and the grandkids, but they've got time, and I trust the Lord to carry on being good to us.
S4.do: Keeps doing his job until retirement while training Mitchell and other apprentices. Keeps saving a little and talks with his son about learning to repair the new machines.
S4.quote: I'd probably think it was pushing too fast on a wet bench.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Felix retires before the change, and his faith gives him a settled outlook. His advice to the young is about character and trade skills. He shows quiet professional pride even when imagining a robot doing his job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Kofi and I would both be out of work at Hollow Creek in the same year, and I'd be too old to start over and too young to retire. What would help is the company keeping on the older operators for the hard jobs until we reach our pension, and apprenticeships for the young ones in trades that still need people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the young ones who learn from us. If there's no old dozer driver on the bench, who teaches the next lot what wet ground looks like? You can't download thirty years of mistakes.

headlineQuote: You can't download thirty years of mistakes.
portrait: Felix Okafor is a 58-year-old bulldozer operator at an open-cut coal mine, a church deacon and a patient trainer of young operators. He distrusts new technology, deleted the AI app his grandson installed, and blames distant office decision-makers and red tape rather than machines. He is calm under the plateau, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in 2028, which could take his job and his son's at the same mine. With five or ten years he plans, guides his grandson toward a trade and leans on faith and family to stay at peace.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he and his son would both lose their jobs at the same mine when he is too old to start over and too young to retire.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older operators on for the hard jobs until their pension, and apprenticeships for young people in trades that still need people.
